column9: rashomon spend splits total cost between the main agent and subagents already, so split the refusal breakdown by agent the same way.

In rashomon lessons, a lesson sitting in probation just shows its fire count with no sense of how close it is to proven. Next to each probation lesson, show the confidence bound against the promotion threshold so I can tell a lesson that's one session away from a near one that's nowhere close.
The commit receipt only wires up prepare-commit-msg and post-commit, so add a pre-push hook body too that pushes the notes ref along with the trailer.

Our project's host-novelty file evicts old hosts once it hits its cap, and the fold result already counts how many got evicted on this particular render. What it doesn't do is remember that across renders, so months from now I have no way to tell whether the project's host list has been through a lot of churn or hardly any. Please keep a running lifetime total of evicted hosts in the file itself.
The recurring-corrections list in rashomon audit just stops after a handful of rows with nothing said about the rest, so say how many more there were.
Test-command inference doesn't know what to do with an Elixir project: it has no row for mix.exs. Teach it to infer mix test the way it already does for Cargo.toml and cargo test.

When I compare two sessions on the same task side by side, the report already warns me if the two sides ran different models, which is great because that would make the comparison meaningless. But it says nothing if one side took five turns and the other took forty, which skews the comparison just as badly. I'd like a similar caveat when the two sides' transcripts show a lopsided number of responses. Keep it a caveat like the model one, not a hard failure.

Replaying a session's calls through the hooks tells me how many of the live steer log's fires it reproduced, but not which ones it missed. When the counts don't match, I have to go diff the two lists myself. Report which fires are in the live log but absent from the replay.

The preflight note classifies what a prompt is asking for (add, fix, refactor, and so on), but asking to delete or remove something currently falls into the catch-all other class. Give delete/remove its own class.

The gate reader can tell whether a test run passed or failed for go test, pytest, jest, vitest and cargo, but not for Maven. A mvn test or mvnw test run's own output just comes back unclassified even though its pass/fail lines are no less distinctive than the others already in the table. Add Maven's summary lines so a Java project's gate can go green or red like everyone else's.

When the sandbox's network audit trail breaks off partway through, the printed summary and the machine-readable one disagree about how many lines it couldn't read. The JSON side keeps a running count of them, but the printed report just goes quiet on that number instead of showing it.
A host we've been tracking for ages randomly shows up again as brand new the moment the project's host list gets re-read after an upgrade.

I started a fresh turn that made no tool calls at all, and the end-of-session report still marked it as having a coverage gap. The gap it's pointing at actually happened earlier in the session, in a completely different turn.

We ran the backtest tool to see which steer patterns would have fired on an old session, and the replay came back with fewer fires than we know the session actually produced live. A few of the calls in that transcript failed with their own error, and it looks like the replay treats those exactly like a call the hook never saw at all, skipping them outright instead of replaying them. The live steer log for that same session shows a pattern firing right after one of those failed calls. Can we get the replay to count those properly so a backtest's numbers match what actually happened?

Every once in a while, right after a batch of old sessions gets cleaned up, the very next run picks up recording from the middle of a file instead of redoing the read from the start. It only seems to happen when a lot of new activity got appended right after the cleanup ran.
Running the exact same build-and-test command from the exact same project folder twice in a row sometimes gets filed under two different working directories instead of one.

We run rashomon in a nightly scheduled job as well as in normal interactive sessions. Nobody is watching the nightly job live, it just uploads its logs and somebody might glance at them a day later. But the reminder notes that are only supposed to matter when a person is actually at the keyboard reading the session live are showing up in the nightly job's record exactly as if someone were watching it in real time. It's as if the tool can't tell an unattended overnight run apart from someone sitting at their laptop.

This is a monorepo where the actual backend code with its own working test target lives one directory down from the root. The step that's supposed to guess our test command from the project's own files keeps saying it has no idea what to run, even though a perfectly good target sits right there one level down.

We switch between two projects a lot inside the same Claude Code session, working one for a while then moving to the other without starting a new session. When I come back to the first project later and ask what its last checkpoint was, it tells me there's no previous session recorded for that project at all. But I know for a fact there's an earlier checkpoint for it sitting in that very same session's records, from before we switched away. It's like the search gives up on a whole run the moment the newest thing in it happens to belong to the other project.
A plain settings file that happens to live inside a folder literally named "test" gets tagged the exact same way a real test file would, instead of being treated as configuration.

We've got two separate places in the codebase that decide whether a string looks like a secret -- one guards what gets redacted before it's disclosed, the other guards what the steering text is allowed to show -- and they reimplement the exact same entropy-test math and deny list from scratch, right down to matching comments about where the canonical definition is supposed to live. Pick one as the real implementation and make the other delegate to it instead of carrying a second hand-copied version of the same check.
Status's JSON output and its plain-text printing are interleaved in the same function; split the JSON building out on its own so changing one doesn't risk touching the other's formatting.

Every time we touch the settings file editor we end up scrolling past the raw-JSON parsing and the byte-for-byte re-encoding just to get to the method that edits one hook's entries. The parsing and rendering of a member's raw JSON is clearly its own job from the higher-level "replace this event's array" editing. Split the low-level parse and render helpers into their own file, away from the Document methods that call them, and keep every output byte-identical. Don't change what gets accepted or rejected, just where the code for it lives.

The shell-command checker's write-detection logic (does this command redirect output, use an in-place editor, pipe into tee) lives in the exact same file as its completely separate "is this actually running the tests" skip-flag logic. Split the write-detection functions out into their own file so the two unrelated jobs aren't tangled together, with no change to what either one decides.

The spend summary's output types are declared right in the middle of the file that builds the summary, sandwiched between the function that assembles it and all its private helpers. Move the type declarations into their own file so the shape of what gets reported isn't buried inside the algorithm that produces it.
Pull the baseline-forgetting functions out of the same file as the baseline read and write path into a file of their own, the same way the update logic already got split out.

Reading the rule-verdict code for a forbidden-command rule means wading through the protected-path matching first, because the flag, wrapper and shell detection for whether a command matched the forbidden pattern sits in the same file as the completely different question of whether a path is inside what the rule protects. They don't call into each other beyond the shared orchestration. Split the forbidden-command matching into its own file and leave the protected-path and evidence checks where they are. Keep every verdict identical; this is just making the file easier to navigate.

Almost every category of file we disclose already gets its own small file -- the checkpoints, the learn ledger, the continuity record, and so on each have a file to themselves. A few categories never got that treatment and are still defined inline in the main file, right next to the inventory type and the function that assembles the whole thing by calling all the others. It's inconsistent, and it makes the main file much longer than it needs to be. Give the leftover categories their own files so the main file is left holding just the type and the top-level builder, matching how the rest of the package is already organized.

The little text-formatting helpers that trim a path or format a byte count for the project brief sit in the same file as the much bigger per-fact builder functions, like the one for the test coverage fact or the spec fact. Split the small formatting helpers into their own file, the way the directory-walking code for the brief already lives separately.

Split the per-ecosystem test-framework probes -- the composer, rspec, flutter and dotnet checks -- out of the file that also does the generic CI-config scan and the run-line parser, into a file of their own.
Nobody here runs .NET, so pull the dotnet project detection out of the test-command guesser entirely.
Almost nobody types the command that explains why one steer note fired - it's a holdover from early debugging. Pull it out of the CLI entirely, usage text included.

We dropped the one Rust service months ago and nobody runs cargo test here anymore. Take the cargo pass/fail recognition out of the test-output classifier so it isn't matching noise against a tool we don't use.

The task-preflight note classifies a prompt's verb before it writes anything, and one of the classes is for deploy/release-shaped requests - 'deploy', 'ship', 'release', 'publish' and the like. We don't act differently on a deploy request anywhere downstream, so carrying a whole verb class for it is dead weight that just makes the classifier harder to read. Remove that class of words from the table and let those prompts fall through the same way an unrecognized verb already does. Keep the rest of the table exactly as it is - fix, refactor, test, migrate and document should all still classify the same.
The may-call edges from class-hierarchy analysis are wrong often enough to be noise - delete that analyzer and stop feeding its guesses into the graph.

Detach is supposed to prove that the only thing it changed in the settings file is removing our own hook entries, byte for byte. That check is expensive to reason about and has never once caught a real bug in the two years it's existed - it just compares bytes and decoded JSON and bails if anything else moved. I want it gone: if detach says it removed our entries, that's good enough, we don't need the paranoid byte-for-byte proof anymore. Leave the rest of detach's reporting alone, just stop running that extra verification.

The check that decides whether a continuity briefing was already shown this boundary is adding complexity we don't need - just delete it and let the briefing render every time a session resumes at that boundary.

Right now a gate run arms a session's stale-evidence trigger with a marker file, and every write after that checks the marker before it pays for the expensive judge, disarming it once it's used. I'd rather simplify this: delete the whole arm/disarm marker mechanism and just run the stale-evidence judge on every write, full stop. Yes that means paying the judge's cost more often, but the code that manages the marker file and its races is harder to reason about than the extra calls are expensive. Rip out the file it creates and the three operations that read, write and remove it.
Stop refusing to compare benchmark numbers across Go versions - just delete that guard and let the gate run on whatever toolchain is installed.
We only ever run this hook under Claude Code, so take out the step that flags a payload as coming from Codex. Treat anything that isn't obviously Cursor as Claude Code and move on.

When a tool call gets retried and one of the retries fails, I've noticed the report always keeps the failed attempt no matter which attempt actually ran last or which one has the higher sequence number. That's probably intentional - a transient failure shouldn't get silently overwritten by a later success - but right now nothing pins it down. Can you add a test that covers the case where the failing attempt is the one with the LOWER sequence number and arrives later in the input, so a future change can't accidentally flip the winner to whichever one simply came last? Don't change any product behavior, just lock in what it does today.
Add a test pinning the exact age boundary for keeping a recent run safe from eviction, so a run exactly at the grace cutoff doesn't start getting pulled in by a future off-by-one.

The host list strips the port off a curl URL before recording it, and I want to make sure that's symmetric for a fetch tool call's own URL field. Add a test where the fetch call's URL carries an explicit non-default port and assert the recorded host has the port stripped the same way the shell-command path does.

Pricing lookups resolve a model id to a rate row, and a couple of the model names in the table are prefixes of each other with a dated suffix appended on real transcripts. Please add a test that a longer model name's dated id resolves to its own rate row and never falls back to the shorter prefix's row, since that would quietly misprice every session on the newer model.
Add a fuzz test for the secret redaction that just asserts it never panics, even on malformed UTF-8 input.

The function that keeps the last N bytes of a long string value uses a fixed-size ring buffer under the hood, and for anything longer than a couple of buffer-fulls it has to wrap around more than once while it's being filled. I went looking for a test that writes enough short pieces to make the buffer wrap at least twice and didn't find one - everything I saw only wraps once. Can you add a test like that, checking the bytes come back in the right order and any partial character left at the wrap point is dropped rather than returned as garbage? No behavior change, just closing the gap in coverage.
Add a test pinning the sort order across the known tier spellings plus one the platform log format has no word for, so the ordering can't silently drift.

The symbol-matching similarity score is defined as zero over zero when both symbols have no tokens at all, specifically so nothing can clear whatever threshold is in use. Add a direct test for that empty-against-empty case so a later refactor can't accidentally make it divide by zero or return something a threshold check would admit.

Session ids over the stored byte cap, or ones that would make the JSON writer escape a character, get swapped for a digest instead of being written raw. Add a table test across ids right at that byte cap, over it, and ones with characters that force the escape path, and confirm the digest a given id gets is the same every time it's computed.

The transcript scanner has a fast path for reading a record's timestamp that only accepts calendar days up to 28 - anything later in the month has to fall through to the slower general parser. I can't find a test that actually exercises a transcript line timestamped on the 29th, 30th or 31st, so I don't know whether that fallback path is even being hit in practice or would quietly misbehave. Please add a test with a record timestamped near the end of a long month and confirm the scan still finds the needle it's looking for in that record. Keep it to tests - the parsing logic itself shouldn't need to change for this.

The per-turn digest build is reading every gap record in the store each time, then throwing away everything that isn't this session's. On a host with a lot of history that's a full store scan on every single turn. Can we scope that read to just the current session before it ever gets filtered?

Every time the call graph resyncs, it reloads and re-parses every package in every module, even when only one file in one package actually changed. I watched it redo a full load on a monorepo-sized tree after a one-line edit in a single package, and that's the slow part of the sync by a wide margin. We already write a digest per file when we save the graph, so there should be enough information lying around to skip a package whose files all still match their last digest. Can we wire that comparison in before the loader decides a package needs reloading, instead of reloading everything unconditionally on any tree change?

Running a backtest over a folder of recorded sessions is slow because it replays them one at a time, start to finish, even though each session is completely independent of the others. Can we fan that out so sessions replay concurrently instead of in a single sequential loop?

The pair comparison tool is supposed to just look at two specific sessions, but under the hood it walks every transcript file across every project on the machine, twice, once to find each side's session, before it throws almost all of that away. On a machine with months of Claude Code history that's a lot of wasted directory walking and file opening for what should be two lookups. The symptom is it visibly pausing for a couple of seconds before printing anything, scaling with how much unrelated history is sitting around, not with the size of the two sessions being compared. I'd like the discovery step scoped down so it isn't re-walking the whole machine's history for a two-session comparison.

Building a report across a bunch of sessions re-reads and rescans the whole sandbox trail file from scratch for every single session in the run, instead of once for the whole report. With a long trail and a big session list that adds up fast. Can that be read once and reused across sessions instead of once per session?
Resolving just a handful of symbol names for a prompt still ends up reading the entire call-graph log off disk every time; can that be made proportional to the few names it's actually looking for?

The obligations ledger in the report rebuilds its family lookup from scratch for every single obligation, rescanning the full gate and verdict lists each time instead of indexing them once up front. On a session with a lot of obligations that's a visibly quadratic chunk of report time. Can that be turned into a single indexing pass instead of a nested rescan per row?
The hygiene scan walks every file in the tree one at a time on a single thread; can it check files concurrently so a full scan doesn't take as long on a big tree?

Finding the last boundary marker at the start of a session reads the whole transcript from the top down, line by line, even though all we actually want is the very last match near the end of the file. On a long-running session with a big transcript that's a full forward scan just to find one line close to the tail. We already have a tail-reading approach elsewhere that opens a section near the end of a big file instead of reading it all from the start; I'd like this boundary lookup to use that same kind of approach instead of a full top-to-bottom pass. Keep the behavior identical when there's no boundary marker at all.

The end-of-turn summary parses every steer-log line for the session twice, once to total up what was delivered and once again to work out what was actually told to me versus missed; can the second pass build on what the first one already parsed instead of re-reading the same lines?

We want to pilot rashomon on a build box with zero outbound network access. install.sh always reaches out to GitHub for the release archive and checksums.txt -- can it accept a release tarball and checksums file already sitting on disk and verify the SHA-256 against them instead of fetching anything?

Our macOS binaries still aren't signed, so a Homebrew cask is off the table for now. README already tells people there's no Homebrew formula at all, which is turning away Linux users who have nothing to do with the signing problem. The .goreleaser.yml comment explaining why the old brews block was ripped out says a public tap could carry a plain formula that serves Linux today, kept separate from the signed-cask path for later. Can we set up that formula in a new public tap and wire the release job to push to it, so brew install works somewhere before signing is sorted out?

scripts/claude-rashomon.ps1 only looks in go\bin and on PATH for the rashomon binary, but the POSIX launcher also checks a user-local bin directory first -- bring the two in line so a Windows install isn't missed.

Now that people install rashomon through the plugin marketplace instead of building it themselves, rashomon-sessionstart.sh's 'binary not found anywhere' line only tells the assistant to offer /rashomon, which assumes a local build exists to run. Can the message also point at enabling the plugin when no binary turns up at all?

measure1 now runs pytest-oracled tasks through a task's RUNNER file, which is great. But I don't think the positive control actually works for them: scripts/measure1_control_prompt.txt is a fixed prompt that names go.mod so the task-preflight note has something to find, and a pytest task's repo is a Python project with no go.mod at all. That means the G1c positive control probably comes back empty on every pytest task, not because steering failed but because the control prompt can never fire there. Can we add a second control prompt that names something a pytest task's repo is guaranteed to have, and have measure1.sh pick the right one off the task's RUNNER file?

demo1.sh is a great walkthrough of a normal recorded session, but every time someone asks what the hook lines print when recording is paused I end up explaining it by hand. Could we add a fourth beat, or a sibling script, that pauses the store first and then runs the same kind of call through the installed lines, masked the same deterministic way the existing turns are?

FuzzREC_OnePassEqualsTwoPass in internal/store found a new failing input, and the entropy scan is flagging a placeholder value in the saved seed as a possible secret even though it isn't one -- add an excusing entry for it to test/tools/hygiene/reviewed.txt the way the existing fuzz-seed rows are written.

install.sh already tells Windows users to just run it inside WSL, but CONTRIBUTING's Known limitations section still reads like Windows installs don't work there at all. Add a line pointing out the WSL path works today, so a contributor doesn't mistake it for covered by the same caveat as a native Windows install.

docs/store-schema.json is thorough on the field-by-field rules, but it's still slow going for a new integration. There's no single worked example anywhere in it -- say, a declaration record next to the execution and terminal records it actually pairs with in one run. Hand-typing one risks it drifting from what the store really writes the first time a field changes. Could we add a short worked example per record kind, built from one of internal/store's own test fixtures so it stays provably accurate?
We're cutting 1.2.0 next -- bump the version string in plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json off the alpha tag.
When the spend estimate prices a cache write, why does it charge a different rate than it would for a cache read of the same tokens?

At the start of a session, rashomon lists which directories under the repo hold Go packages, as part of what it prints to the user. In a huge monorepo I'd expect that scan to be capped somewhere. Where's the cutoff, and what does that line say once the scan hits it?

A teammate's prompt had a couple of Japanese words mixed into an otherwise ordinary English request, right next to a few file names they wanted touched. The task-preflight note built from that prompt didn't point at any of those names. Does the scanner that pulls identifiers out of a prompt choke on the non-ASCII run, or drop it cleanly without touching the ASCII tokens around it?

I'm reading the piece of the Stop evaluation that checks the platform obligations against a logged fact file from a separate build tool. It parses that log with its own small decoder instead of calling into the shared decoder the rest of that tool's commands use. Is that a real boundary someone drew on purpose, or just something nobody got around to tying together? And if that log came from a newer version of the fact-logging tool with a header this reader has never seen, what does the obligations check do with it -- silently skip the family, or call the whole read unknown?

A subagent's run never seems to get a steer line surfaced from its gate output, even though the main session's harness mirror has been trusted for weeks on this machine. Why does a subagent call stay excluded from the verified channel when the main agent's already cleared?
Why does `rashomon brief` print nothing at all right after a compaction, when it prints a full brief on a fresh session start?

The commit receipt docs say this tool never shells out to run git itself. But `rashomon receipt` still produces a trailer line and expects a git note somewhere to carry the actual checkpoint record. If no git process ever runs here, where does that note's content actually get written from? And what ties the trailer's digest back to it, so the two can't quietly drift apart from each other?
Why does the tool decide which directory is a project's identity by walking up for a .git marker instead of normalizing the repository's own git remote URL?

A hook entry point needs to tell whether the harness actually calling it matches the one its entry was installed for, and from what I can tell there's exactly one place in the whole hook pipeline that asks the harness detector that question on real callers. Every other call site either doesn't ask at all or goes through that same spot. Was that centralization deliberate, so every caller gets the exact same answer to a mismatch, or could each entry point just as well run its own check against the raw payload? What would actually break if a second caller started asking the detector directly?

I found a fully built secret-redaction helper in the tree -- its own deny list, its own entropy test over token shapes -- but grepping the binary's actual call sites turns up nothing that imports it. Why isn't it wired into anything that ships today, and where did it come from?
detachTarget quietly falls back to whatever install this machine's store already points to when I pass --install with an empty value, instead of telling me that's not a usable install id.

SDKRecording returns false whenever the file it reads fails to parse, exactly the same as when someone genuinely answered no to recording Agent SDK calls.\nI'm trying to work out why a customer's SDK traffic never gets recorded and I can't tell a corrupted file from an honest refusal from the one bool it gives back.\nCan it at least distinguish those two cases for whoever's debugging?

gapsInWindow hands back a gap from anywhere in the session under a turn that has no declarations of its own, with nothing on the gap to say the match was a session-wide guess rather than something that actually happened during that turn.

LastBoundary only ever returns the transcript's last compact_boundary record.
A session that's been compacted three or four times in one long conversation just gives me the most recent one, with no way to see where the earlier compactions landed.
I'm trying to build something that shows a user every point their context got summarized, not only the most recent cut.
Can it return the whole list of boundaries it already scans past instead of throwing the earlier ones away?

CounterKey keys a harness mismatch count by the exact detected id string, so a genuinely-positive Claude Code detection and a merely-presumed one land in two separate buckets in the saved counts.

costOf lumps five-minute and one-hour cache writes into one cache-write total, so there's no way to see how much of a session's bill is the pricier one-hour cache writes versus the cheaper five-minute ones.

internal/verify/evaluate.go treats every known gate as required the moment a project has no index yet, so a brand-new clone's very first Stop already demands every gate be green before anyone has run anything twice. That's a rough welcome for a fresh repository, and it doesn't match how index.go matures an existing family: a family only becomes required after RequiredSessions sightings within its window. Give a project with no index yet, or one still below RequiredSessions for every family, the same grace an established project gets instead of treating every gate as required from the very first Stop. Keep today's behavior once the index actually exists.

internal/recap/mistakes.go lumps every finding that reached nobody into one Missed bucket, whether it's a genuine miss or a nudge that decide suppressed below its event's floor (ruleNoChannel). internal/settings/diff.go's ValuesFreeDiff only elides values, not keys, and we just had a managed settings key itself be a literal API token someone pasted in by hand -- ValuesFreeDiff printed it straight into a bug report. Elide an object key the same way once it looks secret-shaped.
Bump internal/platform/digests.go's maxSourceBytes past 8 MiB so our generated client files stop reading as stale on every pgraph sync.

internal/learn/ledger.go's Open signs all three state files together under one manifest, so if just labels.ndjson gets touched by something outside this package, every lesson in the project gets quarantined back to proposed, not just whatever that file actually covers. Split internal/shape/masked.go's MaskedBuild into separate lint, typecheck and scan values instead of lumping all three runner kinds into one.

internal/spec/discover.go's Locations only lists MaxWalkDepth candidate spec.json paths climbing from cwd toward root, nearest first. Either raise MaxWalkDepth or have Locations guarantee root's own candidate survives even when the climb from cwd would otherwise be cut short.

internal/brief/walk.go's walkGo skips vendor, testdata and dot/underscore-prefixed directories, but it still walks straight into node_modules in our JS-heavy repos and burns its whole MaxWalkEntries budget there before it reaches the Go packages. Can we add an internal/triagerank package that scores each mistake kind by how often it's recurred across past sessions, so the recap leads with the worst offender instead of whatever happened to be last?

Add an internal/armhistory package that keeps a running count of how many sessions have landed on each arm, since a measure pair's one-off comparison today has no way to say whether its result is typical.

We need a new internal/receiptverify package that re-hashes the checkpoint pulled back off a commit's git note and checks it against the commit receipt, so we can tell a tampered note from an untouched one.

The platform impact read currently just says which package families changed on this run. gateinfer's ecosystem defaults (npm, composer, dotnet, flutter and the rest) are scattered as literals through the inference code. Seed's correction rows are ordered by how often a signature recurred, but that treats a typo retry the same as a repeated rejection. After `rashomon purge` runs there's no single line summarizing what actually happened. Add an internal/purgereport package that turns a purge plan into one line naming the bytes freed and what was deliberately left behind, so the command has something short to print at the end.

Right now the spend numbers we show are always a look back over the last few days. Can you add a new internal/spendforecast package that takes the daily totals spend already reads and projects a month-end figure from them, clearly labelled as a projection and not a bill. harness.Caps answers 'no' for every capability on Cursor and Codex today, and the comment next to it says that's because there's no per-harness lever routing yet, not because those tools can't do it. The disclose package's Default inventory has a comment saying Entries can't be filled in yet because nothing names whether an event prints to nobody, the user alone, or the user and the model. Our steering-message renderer refuses to send a value that looks like a leaked secret, and so does the code that scrubs captured test fixtures -- turns out they each carry their own copy of the exact same deny-list regex and the same forty-character key check, word for word. When we add a new leaked-token shape we always forget one of the two places. Fold the renderer's copy onto the one the fixture scrubber already uses.

There's a little three-line file our dependency-graph sync writes next to its log and digests every run, just enough to say "this log and this digests file are the pair from one sync, trust them together" -- our side reads it back before trusting either. Right now if a sync gets interrupted partway through, our side just reports nothing was ever synced; a person can't tell that apart from a sync that was refused outright for a real reason, like the log coming out too big. Add a short reason code to that little file so a refused sync says why, the way a refused write already explains itself elsewhere in this codebase. Just keep the file's own version marker moving together with the format change -- it's declared twice today, once on the writing side and once on the reading side, with no shared code between them since they're in separate modules.

We just switched one backend's tests over to a different test runner, and now a run that actually failed through it still shows green in the session report -- like nothing in the pipeline that watches for a masked exit status has ever heard of this runner. Teach the output classifier, the hook that records which runner ran, and the gate evaluator about its pass and fail shape the same way they already know the ones we do support.

The rule that decides whether an approved lesson is "about" the file you're currently touching scans the lesson's text for anything that looks like a path, using its own little definition of what counts as a path-shaped word. If that scanner's idea of a path token ever changes, this copy won't follow, and a lesson will start missing files it used to catch.

The project brief already prints which instruction files it found at session start -- the root's and the project's, plus the user's own -- with their sizes, right there on screen. We'd like to know, after the fact, what got loaded for a given session, not just what the brief happened to print live. Write an instruction-load record the same way every other session fact gets recorded, and give the installer a matching event to hook into.

The little command-line tool that bakes the perf budgets table into the binary, and the one that rewrites the perf budgets file after a benchmark run to update its reference numbers, each have their own hand-rolled copy of the exact same "walk up from here to the nearest go.mod" helper -- pull it into one place both of them call.

Our holdout assigner is supposed to be the one shared coin-flip every steering feature uses, so "held out" means the same thing everywhere, but the backtest replay tool just hardcodes every session as treatment and never asks it. Leave the before/after check that proves an uninstall only took our entries out alone, but when it comes back false because something else in the settings file changed too, have it say which keys actually differ instead of just reporting a plain mismatch.

A paired measurement run counts regressions, stale evidence and a handful of other pattern lines as findings in the side-by-side comparison, but a credential-spray detection on one side just melts into the ordinary note count instead of standing out. The kept-count record from before install only remembers the top 100 projects by session count, so on a machine with lots of small repos it quietly drops the quieter ones from the before tally — raise that cap without shrinking how many correction rows each project keeps.
